prompt: A page makes 40 **sequential** calls to a backend. Each call does 1 ms of work. The backend moves from the same data centre (0.5 ms round trip) to another region (70 ms round trip). Roughly how long does the page now spend on these calls?

options.explanation: Correct. 40 × (70 + 1) = 2,840 ms. Each sequential call pays the full round trip, so latency multiplies by call count.
Wrong. This is the old figure: 40 × (1 + 0.5) = 60 ms. It ignores the new round-trip time.
Wrong. This adds one 70 ms round trip to the old total, as if all calls shared one round trip. Sequential calls each pay the full latency.
Wrong by a factor of 10; it treats each round trip as 700 ms.

workedExample:
Each sequential call must finish before the next starts, so the page pays the round trip plus the work once per call:

```formula
T = n × (RTT + w)
T_old = 40 × (0.5 ms + 1 ms)
T_old = 60 ms
T_new = 40 × (70 ms + 1 ms)
T_new = 2,840 ms ≈ 2.8 s
where
T: total time the page spends on the calls, in milliseconds (ms)
T_old: the total with the backend in the same data centre
T_new: the total with the backend in another region
n: the number of sequential calls; here 40
RTT: round-trip time, the time for a request to reach the backend and the reply to return, in ms
w: the work the backend does per call; here 1 ms
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
s: second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: every sequential call pays the full round trip, so a 140-fold increase in round-trip time makes the page about 47 times slower.
```

That is the fallacy "latency is zero" in action. Fixes: batch the 40 calls into one, run them in parallel (roughly 71 ms total under the same simplified timing assumptions), or keep chatty services co-located.
